newsitem.title: UK: Volatile European gas oil to slide in '97 - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Volatile European gas oil to slide in '97 - analysts.

text.p: European gas oil prices over the next 12 months are unlikely to revisit five year highs seen in 1996 but the depleted state of industry stocks should continue to create short-term volatility, market analysts say.
A looser heating oil supply/demand balance should pressure crack spreads as well as outright values despite the potential for stock-driven price spikes, they said.
Low sulphur diesel has a steadier outlook because of increasing demand driven by environmental pressure.
"We won't see gas oil anything like as high this year," said Colin Birch, analyst at Purvin & Gertz. "But while it's not as strong as last year, I wouldn't call it bearish."
"I think spreads on average will be lower than this year," said Roger Diwan, senior economist on the global oil market at Washington-based Petroleum Finance Company.

Birch said he saw the gas oil/Brent spread narrowing to about $5 a barrel in December 1997 from $5.85 a barrel in December 1996, based on a projected December 1997 price of $180 a tonne compared to around $217 last December.
The continuing rise of automotive diesel demand has helped keep a lid on the low European stocks created by the repeated draws of recent years and "just-in-time" inventory management.
But the supply disruption caused by last year's mandatory European Union switch to very low sulphur diesel use will not be repeated and this will shave values.

"The scenario of low stocks resulting in increased volatility and higher prices is a near term situation but in 1997 as a whole we'll see the middle distillates crack down compared to 1996," said Jonathan Severs, an analyst at British Petroleum.

With record low consumer stocks and inventories higher up the distribution networks depleted, "there will be big demand at some point," he added. "But the big question is, is it big enough to carry the market? My guess is, 'No'."
"If volumes from the Med don't go to the Far East, and if (European) refiners don't cut runs, then stocks would rise and the overhang would pressure prices."

Swaps prices support a mildly bearish outlook for heating oil. Swaps for the gas oil/Brent crack spread are at $4.75 and $5.35 for the third and fourth quarters of 1997 respectively from $5.18 and $6.42 in 1996.

The swap for physical 0.2 heating oil above the screen is quoted around +$4, +$3 and +$5 for the second, third and fourth quarters of 1997 respectively against +$6, +$3.50 and close to +$4.50 in 1996.

Analysts see a range of other factors combining to pressure values and spreads over 1997. They include growing use of gas for heating, the possibility of slower economic activity as governments tighten public finances to meet monetary union criteria in Europe new Far East refinery capacity mopping up incremental Chinese and Indian demand and little chance of a repeat of the deep freeze of 1995/96.

European moves to cut overcapacity have been offset by big expansion in Asia. South Korea and Thailand added up to 500,000 barrels per day of overall new capacity in 1996 while Europe has cut about 250,000 bpd in the last two years and plans another 60,000 bpd closure in 1997.

End-user heating oil stocks in Germany, the continent's main heating oil market, are still languishing below historical averages at around 56 percent of capacity. But wholesalers and end-users could simply be resisting the high prices to restock in a backwardated market.

Dissenting from the overall view, one trader argued for holding stocks. "Low stocks and high values have established quite a good backwardation in the market, and that is one of the main reasons why we don't have stocks and people don't want to buy to resupply.

"But if you follow simply logic, holding stocks during the winter has proved to be very useful. It seems that people concentrate too much on IPE spreads and gas oil spreads and ignore common sense that in winter you should hold gas oil."
Longer term rising demand for natural gas for heating around the continent is bearish "background noise" for heating oil, Severs said.
"There is some gas substitution already," said Diwan. "It's creeping up every year."
Traders say a late cold snap, coinciding with refiners' switch to maximum gasoline output, could provoke another gas oil price spike and additional volatility.

But overall, argued Diwan, U.S. and European refiners had shown during 1996 that they were able to produce large amounts of middle distillates and switch runs flexibly, "something that was in doubt a year ago" during the big European freeze.
